As a result, they provide a near continuous supply of cooling with only minimal pumping energy. The concept leverages established drilling technologies that have been developed over decades in the oil, gas, and geothermal industries, including directional drilling. Although still in the early stages of conceptualization and development, GeoSWAC offers streamlined system architecture, featuring minimal moving parts, no refrigerants, and significantly lower electricity consumption compared to conventional vapor-compression systems, which suggests strong potential for reliable and resilient operation in regions subject to grid instability or extreme weather events. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Image by Joshua Bauer, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) 1.2 San Juan Metropolitan Area San Juan, the capital and most populous municipality of Puerto Rico, has a tropical rainforest climate with persistently high temperatures and humidity throughout the year. Typical meteorological year 3 (TMY3) data collected at the San Juan–Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport from 1973 to 2005 show that ambient temperatures range from 20.6°C to 35°C (Figure 2) while relative humidity varies between 40% and 100% (Bianchi and Fontanini 2021). These climatic conditions result in substantial and year-round cooling demands, making air conditioning an essential and energy-intensive requirement for buildings across the region. 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. To meet cooling demand, UPR-RP, one of the largest universities in Puerto Rico, operates eight chilled water plants consisting of electric-driven water-cooled vapor-compression chillers, circulating pumps, and distribution loops. While the chilled water plants enable efficient centralized cooling and operational coordination, their reliance on grid electricity emphasizes the importance of enhancing energy resilience, particularly during extreme weather events that can disrupt the power supply. During a technical visit to the island, National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) researchers collected information provided by the Oficina de Planificación y Desarrollo Físico of UPR-RP. The university campus was selected as the type of facility to be evaluated in this study. Figure 2. The references were divided into two categories: subsurface and surface datasets. Regional geology and hydrogeology were primarily sourced from U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) reports and scientific journals, which documented deep, medium, and shallow wells across the north and south coasts.
